config.title: :is() and :where()

intro.title: :is() and :where()
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple webpage to style different types of list items and links using the CSS pseudo-classes `:is()` and `:where()`. You will learn how these selectors help you write cleaner, more efficient CSS by grouping multiple selectors together. The core concept involves understanding selector specificity—how `:is()` adopts the highest specificity in its list, while `:where()` always has zero specificity. You will apply these constructs directly in a CSS file to see their practical effects on HTML elements.
intro.usecase: The :is() and :where() pseudo-classes are essential for writing clean, maintainable CSS in complex web applications. For example, in a dashboard with multiple panels, you can use :is() to apply consistent styling to headings across different sections like 'Recent Activity', 'Analytics', and 'User List' without repeating long selector chains. Similarly, :where() is perfect for theming or component libraries, allowing you to apply base styles to elements like buttons or form inputs within a modal or sidebar without increasing specificity, making it easier to override styles later. These selectors help developers reduce code duplication and manage specificity conflicts in real-world projects like admin panels, e-commerce sites, or design systems.

objectives: Apply the :is() pseudo-class to group multiple selectors for concise styling
Implement the :where() pseudo-class to create zero-specificity selector groups
Construct CSS rules using :is() to target nested elements efficiently
Configure selector lists with :where() to maintain low specificity in complex stylesheets
Manipulate element styling by combining :is() with other pseudo-classes
Integrate :where() into existing CSS to override styles without specificity conflicts
Update legacy CSS selectors by replacing comma-separated lists with :is() for better readability

steps.title: Create a basic HTML structure to style
steps.instruction: Create a simple HTML structure with multiple nested elements that we can target with CSS selectors. Use a div with class 'container' containing a heading, paragraph, and unordered list with three list items.
steps.hint: Start with a div element and add the specified child elements inside it. Remember to use proper HTML nesting.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a basic HTML structure ready to be styled with CSS selectors in the next steps.
successCriteria: A div with class 'container' contains an h1 heading, a paragraph, and an unordered list with three list items.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have all the required elements: a div with class 'container' containing an h1, a p, and a ul with three li items.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a div with class 'container' that contains an h1 heading, a paragraph, and an unordered list with three list items.

steps.title: Add basic styling to understand the starting point
steps.instruction: Add CSS rules to style the HTML elements with basic colors and spacing to establish a visual baseline.
steps.hint: You can add CSS rules for elements like headings, paragraphs, and lists to make them visually distinct.
steps.seedCode:
/* Create your HTML structure here */

/* Add your basic CSS styles here */
steps.expectedOutcome: The HTML elements will have basic visual styling applied, making them easier to distinguish.
successCriteria: CSS rules are added for at least three different HTML element types with properties like color, margin, or padding.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some styles, but try to style at least three different element types for better visual distinction.
steps.feedbackWrong: No CSS rules were added. Please add basic styling to HTML elements like headings, paragraphs, or lists.

steps.title: Style multiple elements with traditional CSS selectors
steps.instruction: Add CSS rules to style the header, main, and footer elements with a light gray background color (#f0f0f0). Use three separate selector rules.
steps.hint: Write three CSS rules: one for the header element, one for the main element, and one for the footer element. Each rule should set the background-color property to #f0f0f0.
steps.expectedOutcome: The header, main, and footer elements will all have the same light gray background color, demonstrating selector repetition.
successCriteria: Three separate CSS rules exist that target header, main, and footer elements, each setting background-color to #f0f0f0.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have three separate rules for header, main, and footer elements, each with background-color: #f0f0f0.
steps.feedbackWrong: write three CSS rules: one for header, one for main, and one for footer, each setting background-color to #f0f0f0.

steps.title: Introduce the :is() pseudo-class selector
steps.instruction: Replace the repetitive traditional selectors from the previous step with a single :is() selector that targets the same elements.
steps.hint: Use the :is() pseudo-class to combine multiple selectors into one. For example, :is(h1, h2, h3) { color: blue; } styles all three heading levels.
steps.expectedOutcome: The CSS file will use :is() selectors instead of comma-separated traditional selectors to apply the same styles.
successCriteria: The traditional comma-separated selectors are replaced with :is() selectors that target the same elements and apply the same styles.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the :is() pseudo-class correctly and targeting all the same elements as before.
steps.feedbackWrong: The traditional selectors should be replaced with :is() selectors. Check the syntax and ensure you're targeting the same elements.

steps.title: Understand :is() specificity behavior
steps.instruction: Add a new CSS rule that uses :is() with a high-specificity selector (like an ID) to demonstrate how it takes the highest specificity, overriding the previous styles.
steps.hint: Create a selector like #special :is(h1, h2, h3) and give it a different color to see the specificity effect.
steps.expectedOutcome: The learner will see how :is() adopts the highest specificity from its arguments, causing elements inside #special to be red instead of navy.
successCriteria: A CSS rule using :is() with an ID selector is added, demonstrating specificity override.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your selector includes an ID (like #special) combined with :is() to demonstrate specificity.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the hint: you need to create a selector with an ID and :is() to show specificity behavior.

steps.title: Introduce the :where() pseudo-class selector
steps.instruction: Replace the traditional CSS selectors for paragraphs, spans, and divs with a single :where() selector that applies the same font-size styling.
steps.hint: Use :where(p, span, div) to target the same elements as before. The syntax is similar to :is() but with different specificity behavior.
steps.expectedOutcome: The CSS will use :where(p, span, div) to apply font-size: 16px to those elements, demonstrating the :where() selector syntax.
successCriteria: The :where() selector is used to target p, span, and div elements with font-size: 16px
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using :where() with the correct syntax: :where(p, span, div) { font-size: 16px; }
steps.feedbackWrong: Use the :where() pseudo-class selector to target p, span, and div elements with font-size: 16px.

steps.title: Understand :where() specificity behavior
steps.instruction: Create a CSS rule that demonstrates how :where() has zero specificity by styling a paragraph element with conflicting selectors.
steps.hint: Use :where() to target a paragraph with a class, then add a more specific selector that overrides it to show the zero specificity effect.
steps.expectedOutcome: The paragraph with class 'special' should be styled with the color from the more specific selector, demonstrating that :where() has zero specificity.
successCriteria: CSS includes a :where() selector targeting paragraphs with a class, and a more specific selector that overrides it to show zero specificity behavior.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have both the :where() selector and a more specific selector that conflicts with it to show the specificity difference.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've created a :where() selector and a conflicting more specific selector to demonstrate the zero specificity behavior.

steps.title: Compare :is() and :where() side by side
steps.instruction: Create a new CSS rule that uses :is() to style all h1, h2, and h3 elements with a background color of lightblue.
steps.hint: Add a new selector using :is() with the element list inside parentheses, then set the background-color property.
steps.expectedOutcome: The :is() selector will be applied to h1, h2, and h3 elements with a lightblue background, demonstrating its normal specificity behavior.
successCriteria: A CSS rule using :is(h1, h2, h3) with background-color: lightblue is added to the stylesheet.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the :is() pseudo-class with the correct syntax: :is(h1, h2, h3) { background-color: lightblue; }
steps.feedbackWrong: The comparison example needs a :is() selector. Try adding :is(h1, h2, h3) with a background-color property set to lightblue.

steps.title: Use :is() and :where() with complex selectors
steps.instruction: Add a new CSS rule that uses :is() with pseudo-classes to style interactive elements.
steps.hint: You can combine :is() with pseudo-classes like :hover or :focus to apply styles to multiple element types when they are in a specific state.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will create a CSS rule using :is() with pseudo-classes to demonstrate how these selectors work with more complex patterns.
successCriteria: The CSS contains a rule using :is() with at least one pseudo-class (like :hover, :focus, or :active) that targets multiple element types.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your selector uses :is() with at least one pseudo-class and targets multiple element types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSS rule doesn't match the requirements. Check that you're using :is() with a pseudo-class and targeting multiple elements.

steps.title: Practical use case: resetting styles with :where()
steps.instruction: Add a CSS reset rule using :where() to remove default margins and padding from all heading and paragraph elements with zero specificity.
steps.hint: Use :where() with a selector list containing h1, h2, h3, p, and set margin and padding to 0.
steps.expectedOutcome: A CSS rule using :where() that resets margins and padding for h1, h2, h3, and p elements with zero specificity impact.
successCriteria: The code includes a :where() selector with h1, h2, h3, p and sets both margin and padding to 0.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your :where() selector includes all required elements (h1, h2, h3, p) and sets both margin and padding to 0.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSS reset rule is missing or incorrect. Remember to use :where() with a selector list and set margin and padding to 0.
